extracted.intended_audience: European patent practitioners / EPO applicants / patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards on when and how the description of a European patent application should be adapted following claim amendments (Article 84 EPC), including related risks (added matter Article 123(2)), case law tensions, and recommended alignment with PCT/national practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to remove "inconsistencies" after claim amendments (EPO Guidelines F-IV 4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2021 revision of the EPO Guidelines F-IV 4.3 (i) - (iii) requires adapting the description after claim amendments to remove 'inconsistencies' between the description and the amended claims, based on an expanded interpretation of the support requirement of Article 84 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the EPO Guidelines' stated practice that has triggered controversy; the page notes it is an expanded interpretation of the support requirement and has led to conflicting Board of Appeal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation needed only if inconsistency makes claim language unclear (T 2194/19 approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inconsistency or contradiction between description and claims justifies adaptation only if parts of the description make the language of the claims unclear; otherwise not justified when the language of the claims is clear in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: T 2194/19 equates 'inconsistency' and 'contradiction' and ties the requirement to the clarity requirement of Article 84 in combination with support. Practical implication: do not require deletion of unclaimed embodiments unless the Division shows they make the claims unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on the Examining Division to show inconsistency causes doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: The Examining Division must explain why the inconsistency it requires the applicant to remove would make the language of the claims unclear; mere absence of coverage of an embodiment by the claims is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Division must make a specific showing that the inconsistency 'causes doubt' about claim language; hypothetical or potential doubts ('could cause') are not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Does cause doubt" threshold (not "could cause doubt")
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for removing inconsistencies is not justified by reference to hypotheticals (i.e. if the inconsistency could cause doubt). It is only justified if the inconsistency causes doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a present-tense, actual-doubt standard when assessing whether description elements must be deleted or amended; speculative possibilities are insufficient grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with PCT ISPE Guidelines (section 5.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT ISPE Guidelines provide an approach paralleling the sensible approach that description adaptation is not justified by mere hypotheticals; practitioners would benefit if EPO practice regarding the EPO phase was brought in line with the PCT Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling euro‑PCT applications (including when EPO is ISA), consider PCT ISPE §5.29 as persuasive guidance; convergence would improve predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO's interpretation invoking a 'precise determination' of scope (T 3097/19 critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: T 3097/19 shifts rationale from support to an interpretation of the first sentence of Article 84 calling for a 'precise determination' of the scope of protection, which the author considers to go far beyond the clarity requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach conflicts with settled case law that claims may be broad without violating clarity; be wary of Boards invoking an elevated 'precision' standard to justify description adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must mention all essential features — requirement for claims, not description (GL F-IV 4.3 (ii), T 32/82)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is established case law that a claim must mention all essential features. This is a requirement for the claims, not for the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate claim content obligations with requirements to rewrite the description; essential-feature requirements should be addressed in claim drafting rather than by wholesale deletion from the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boards must explain departures from Guidelines (RPBA 2020 Article 20(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: RPBA 2020 Article 20(2) suggests that the Board shall provide an explanation when it departs from the Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Boards adopt reasoning that departs from EPO Guidelines, expect and request a clear explanation of why; lack of explanation undermines predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of creating Article 123(2) new matter issues when amending the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive amendments of the description have the potential of creating Article 123(2) issues because admissibility of amendments is assessed by reference to the content of the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substantive description amendments where possible; adaptions risk adding matter not originally disclosed and can lead to revocation (illustrated by T 1473/19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical risk from Examining Division amendments at Rule 71(3) stage without applicant consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining Divisions' frequent practice of making amendments at Rule 71(3) stage to speed up the process, without prior consultation with applicants, compounds risks since the applicant remains responsible for the granted text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor Rule 71(3) communications closely; object to or challenge late-stage amendments if they create new-matter or other adverse consequences, balancing delay/cost considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO practice may improperly interfere with national courts' role under Article 69 EPC
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO's asserted 'legal security' justification for deleting unclaimed embodiments can be seen as an attempt to interfere with national courts' competence to interpret claims of granted patents under Article 69 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious that description amendments intended to influence post‑grant claim interpretation may overreach the EPO's remit and generate conflict with national practice and case law (e.g., Pemetrexed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deleting unclaimed embodiments creates prosecution-estoppel/disclaimer risks (national courts' consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO's objective in deleting unclaimed embodiments may be to create the equivalent of a disclaimer or prosecution estoppel preventing a patentee from recapturing ground; national courts have generally rejected such overreaching consequences (Pemetrexed and many national decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that deleting embodiments during prosecution will prevent broader claim interpretation by national courts; litigation outcomes may still allow broader constructions or equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation in examination should be broadest possible and without relying on the description (T 2502/19 principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be taken by themselves and tested against the broadest possible or objectively reasonable construction which would occur to the skilled reader; Article 84 does not require reliance on other parts of the application documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examination claim interpretation is independent of the description, adapting the description is often irrelevant to clarity under Article 84; focus on claim drafting and clarity rather than description redaction for examination purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of words like 'substantially'/'approximately' (GL F-IV 4.7) can cause new-matter problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The ban on words such as 'substantially' and 'approximately' required by Guidelines F-IV 4.7 can create issues: if an Examining Division deletes 'substantially' but the description never discloses the strict form, this may be considered inadmissible new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful when responding to objections that call for removing such qualifiers; deletion may change the claimed subject-matter scope and create Article 123(2) issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: National courts may find new matter if an amendment alters claim interpretation (UK Manual Section 76)
rubrics_metrics.description: National courts may find there is new matter whenever an amendment alters the interpretation of the claims by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider national practice and manuals (e.g., UK Manual of patent practice Section 76) when deciding whether to accept or implement description or claim amendments that might affect subsequent claim construction by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diverging Board decisions undermine predictability; consider referral to Enlarged Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing divergences within the Boards of Appeal on the rationale and scope of the description-adaptation requirement create legal uncertainty; users have called for a referral to the Enlarged Board of Appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Board case law is conflicting on Article 84/description adaptation, counsel may consider seeking clarity via petitions for referral or by relying on more applicant‑friendly decisions when arguing before Divisions/Boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek convergence of practice across EPO, national offices and PCT through EPO 'Convergence of practice programme'
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be desirable to examine description adaptation within the EPO's 'Convergence of practice programme' with the aim of defining a common, harmonised practice across European patent offices; PCT ISPE §5.29 could be helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for or reference convergence initiatives and PCT guidance when resisting burdensome EPO-only practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate support requirement (Article 84) with added-matter assessment (Article 123) — be mindful of interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO's reliance on Article 84 to require description adaptation seems to conflate support/clarity considerations with added-matter concerns under Article 123; adaptation may paradoxically create 123(2) problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing objections, keep distinct the legal bases (clarity/support vs admissibility/added matter) and avoid amendments that solve one problem by creating another.
